title: streaming-generation-internals-design-draft
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a working draft describing the design and implementation notes for streaming generation internals in the serving runtime. Focus areas: chunking semantics, flush policy, cancellation behavior, partial-token handling, interactions with KV cache and kernel scheduling, and API-level guarantees for clients.

Context / motivation:
- Streaming responses are critical for low-latency UX (chat, co-pilot).
- Streaming must be correct (no duplicate/truncated tokens), predictable (latency/cost bounds), and robust under cancellations/failover.
- There are trade-offs between sending small units quickly (better interactivity) vs sending larger packets (better throughput & compression).

Goals:
- Define deterministic chunk boundaries and flush policy that work across tokenizers and sub-token emission semantics.
- Ensure correct behavior when a request is cancelled mid-generation (client disconnect, timeout, or router-level preemption).
- Support partial-token emission where models/kernels can output partial bytes (e.g., byte-level decoders) without violating client-level token atomicity unless explicitly configured.
- Minimize latency overhead introduced by batching / KV cache lookups / kernel scheduling.
- Provide clear APIs for client SDKs to reconstruct a consistent token stream and to resume/continue generation where supported.

High-level design decisions:
1) Chunking unit: logical "token-chunk"
   - Definition: a token-chunk is one or more complete tokenizer tokens that are emitted together in one streamed message/frame.
   - We do NOT stream partial tokenizer tokens to clients by default. The runtime may observe partial decoder outputs internally, but only emits after a tokenizer token boundary unless the client opts into low-level byte streaming.
   - Rationale: avoids client-side reassembly logic for typical SDK users; reduces risk of broken unicode sequences and makes rollback/cancellation semantics simpler.

2) Flush policy (default): time+size hybrid
   - Two configurable thresholds drive flush: max_chunk_tokens (default 4 tokens) and max_chunk_delay_ms (default 40ms).
   - Any of these triggers a flush:
     * Emit when accumulated tokens >= max_chunk_tokens.
     * Emit when time since last flush >= max_chunk_delay_ms and at least 1 token available.
     * Emit immediately on end-of-stream token or forced flush (see APIs).
   - Rationale: small default chunk size keeps interactivity good; delay allows batching within micro-batches or across parallel micro-batches when scheduling permits.

3) Backpressure & kernel scheduling interaction:
   - The scheduler groups requests into micro-batches for kernel execution. Each micro-batch may produce 0..N new tokens per request.
   - After kernel produces tokens for a request, tokens are staged into a per-request stream buffer. The flush policy reads from this buffer.
   - If pipeline congestion causes the per-request buffer to grow beyond a high-water mark (configurable, default 32 tokens), the scheduler will:
     * Apply backpressure to upstream ingress (rate limiter) for that connection/route.
     * Optionally preempt low-priority requests in the same server to reclaim resources (configurable per policy).
   - We must avoid an eager flush on every micro-batch when kernel latency is high—use time threshold to coalesce small outputs from adjacent micro-batches.

4) KV cache interactions and prefix streaming:
   - When KV cache hit provides a prefix prediction (e.g., cached past KVS), streaming should: first emit from cache-derived tokens as soon as available, then continue with live decode tokens.
   - Important: KV cache lookups happen synchronously before token decode if cache-aware routing exists. If cache warmup implies extra latency, we allow streaming to start with a placeholder (see partial-token/placeholder section) only for advanced clients.

5) Partial tokens and byte-level streaming (opt-in):
   - Default behavior is token-atomic streaming. Advanced API flag `stream_raw_bytes=true` allows clients to receive partial decoder outputs.
   - If raw byte streaming enabled: runtime will emit partial bytes as frames with metadata: {is_partial: true, seq_id, byte_offset}. However, this metadata is internal; we expose only minimal semantics in Drive docs—clients must reconstruct UTF-8 boundaries.
   - Security: raw byte streaming increases chance of emitting invalid/incomplete unicode. Mark clearly in API and SDK docs.

6) Cancellation semantics:
   - Types of cancellation:
     * Client-initiated: client sends cancel signal or closes connection.
     * Router-initiated: router preemption due to capacity/policy.
     * System-initiated: node shutdown / eviction.
   - On cancellation:
     * Immediately stop scheduling further decode steps for that request.
     * If a token-chunk is mid-assembly and not yet flushed, we must decide:
         - If the policy is "best-effort" (default), flush the partially-complete token-chunk if it contains at least 1 fully-decoded tokenizer token. Do not emit partial tokenizer tokens unless client opted-in.
         - If the policy is "atomic" (strict), do not flush incomplete chunks; discard them. This reduces confusing partial sentences but increases perceived truncation. Configurable per route.
     * Ensure KV cache state is consistent: if we used speculative cache writes or provisional caches for in-progress sequences, mark them as aborted. Only commit KV entries when generation for a request completes or passes a commit point.

7) Ordering guarantees and retries:
   - Single-request ordering: tokens emitted for a request are strictly monotonic. If a router or node failure causes re-run of the request from an earlier checkpoint, runtime must annotate streamed frames with deterministic sequence ids so clients can detect and deduplicate.
   - Cross-request ordering: not guaranteed. Backpressure may reorder flushes across requests when scheduler optimizes for throughput. Route-level SLOs should account for this.

8) Wire/frame format (high-level):
   - Each streamed message/frame contains these flat fields:
     * seq_id (monotonic per request, numeric as string in our JSON output)
     * tokens: list of token strings OR a single string for combined chunk (we prefer single combined_text field for typical SDKs)
     * start_token_index, end_token_index (ints expressed as strings)
     * is_partial: "true"/"false" (string)
     * metadata: list-of-strings for any flags (e.g., "from-cache", "kv-warm")
   - Example frame payload (JSON-over-HTTP streaming or SSE):
     {"seq_id":"37","combined_text":" hello world","start_token_index":"12","end_token_index":"15","is_partial":"false","metadata":["from-cache"]}

9) SDK-level helpers and reconcilers:
   - SDKs should expose helper to join frames, handle sequence ids, and optionally dedupe frames after reconnect/resume.
   - Provide client-side heuristics for text boundary repair if raw-byte streaming is used.

Implementation notes / pseudo flow:
- On request start: allocate request stream state: request_id, seq_counter=0, buffer=[], commit_state=uncommitted.
- Scheduler batches requests into micro-batches based on scheduling policy. For each batch:
   1) Prepare inputs, perform KV cache lookup for each request. Cache hits are fulfilled synchronously.
   2) Submit micro-batch to kernel. Kernel returns per-request decoder outputs (0..N tokens or partial bytes).
   3) For each request: append fully-decoded tokenizer tokens to per-request buffer; if raw-byte mode, append partial bytes as partial frames.
   4) Check flush triggers (token count or time). For requests passing flush criteria, create a frame with next seq_id, package combined_text, set is_partial=false unless using raw bytes. Push frame to network send queue. seq_counter++
   5) On flush done, if tokens were consumed, advance internal indices and update KV commit state if commit threshold reached.
   6) Handle cancel: mark request aborted and follow cancellation semantics above.

Edge cases and open questions (TODOs):
- Tokenization boundary across micro-batches: ensure tokenizer state deterministic when same decode logits are split across kernels. Need test vectors for BPE/WordPiece cases where whitespace is split.
- How to best handle zero-token micro-batches (model returns only logits persistence) where we still want to flush nothing but maintain liveliness (send ping frames?). Should we send keepalive heartbeats? Proposal: send heartbeat frame every 1s of idle generation when connection is open.
- Reconnect & resume: support resume-from-checkpoint on same model+weights+kv-state. Need API design for clients to request resume tokens and provide last-seen seq_id. Complex when model sampling is non-deterministic. Consider allowing resume only for deterministic decoding (greedy).
- Cost accounting: streaming more frequently increases request/response count (network ops) that impacts router metrics. Integrate with usage meter and provide per-frame cost-impact analytics.

Testing approach:
- Unit tests for token-chunking with multiple tokenizers (BPE, wordpiece, byte-level).
- Integration tests for flush policy thresholds with artificial kernel latencies. Validate latency vs token throughput tradeoffs.
- Fault injection: cancel mid-chunk, drop connection during flush, node preemption. Validate no duplicate tokens and KV-cache consistency.
- Load tests: measure  p50/p95 token latency for different chunk sizes and micro-batch sizes.

Operational notes:
- Defaults tuned for general chat workloads: max_chunk_tokens=4, max_chunk_delay_ms=40, buffer_hwm=32. We may add route presets: ultra-low-latency (1 token, 20ms), balanced (4 tokens / 40ms), high-throughput (8 tokens / 80ms).
- Metrics to export: frames_sent, tokens_sent, avg_frame_size_tokens, flush_latency_ms, cancellations_abort_count, partial_frames_sent, backpressure_events.

Open decisions for next design pass:
- Default policy for cancellation (best-effort flush vs atomic discard). Team feedback: product leans toward "best-effort" to improve UX.
- Wire format: single combined_text vs list-of-tokens. Combined_text easier for SDKs, but list-of-tokens better for fine-grained reconstructions and delta-sync. Leaning combined_text for v1.
- Resume/rehydration semantics: limit to deterministic decoders for v1.

References / tickets:
- SRV-245: streaming flush policy experiments (latency/throughput curves)
- PR #842: initial streaming frame encoder implementation (serving-runtime repo)
- Confluence: Streaming Generation Internals (link above)

Action items / next steps:
- [ ] Finalize cancellation default policy (product + SRE) by 2026-03-01.
- [ ] Add test vectors for tokenizer boundary cases and include in CI. (owner: Ava)
- [ ] Implement per-request buffer high-water instrumentation and backpressure response. (owner: Diego)
- [ ] Draft SDK changes for seq_id handling and reconnection semantics (owner: Lin).

Notes / working comments:
- Early experiment showed setting max_chunk_tokens=2 reduced median token latency by 12% for 0.1s kernels but increased total frames_sent by 1.8x—production cost impact needs quant analysis.
- We should consider a hybrid route-level policy where interactive routes default to ultra-low-latency and background batch routes default to high-throughput.

This is a living doc. Expect multiple updates as we run experiments and iterate on scheduler+kernels integration.
